name: Robin Hood
sources: Bord, Janet, and Colin Bord. The Secret Country: An interpretation of the folklore of ancient sites in the British Isles. (New York: Walker and Co., 1976), 76.
Briggs, Katherine M. The Folklore of the Cotswolds. London: B. T. Batsford, Ltd., 1974, 35.
Spence, Lewis. The Minor Traditions of British Mythology. (New York: Benjamin Blom, Inc., 1972), 106.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Robin Hood is a hero of British folklore. He took from the rich and offered to the poor. The tales may hold some truth. He is said to have lived with Maid Marian and a band of outlaws in the woods of England. The band included Little John and Friar Tuck. Many outlaws did dwell in those forests. One of them caught the people's fancy. The Robin Hood story passed down more in writing than in talk, and the upper class prized it more than the lower. The man in the story may be Robin Locksley, born in Brandfield Parish in Hallamshire. He wounded his stepfather by accident. He fled to Loxley forest. There among the trees he came upon a tall hermit named Little John. A grave opened there in 1784 held a thigh bone thirty inches long, then was buried again and lost. Some scholars tie Robin to the Green Man, a being of woods and growth. Under this view he took the title Robin of the Wood. He answered to Jack-in-the-Green as well, reigning as May's king beside Queen Maid Marian. Such figures joined the Beltane feast and the high-summer rites of late June. A horn dance still survives at Abbots Bromley, where men circle a woman dressed as Maid. One legend sets Robin and Little John at a leaping contest. Robin struck Wormsley Hill with his heel and broke off Butthouse Knap. Little John's jump shaped Pyon Hill. Together these slopes are the hills called Robin Hood's Butts. Robin still guards the district. Diggers found their spades scattered and gorse clothing over each fresh hole. Such pranks are fairy work, so the tale links Robin to the Otherworld.
